items.title: Thomas More's 'Utopia' (1516) coined the word
items.claim: What did Thomas More publish in 1516?

options.text: A history of the Wars of the Roses

'Utopia' — a Latin work describing a fictional island society, coining the word from Greek 'ou-topos' (no place) and 'eu-topos' (good place); a humanist critique of European politics, property and religion
A defence of the medieval feudal system

items.reveal_title: No place that critiques every place
items.reveal:
'Utopia' was written in Latin and first printed at Louvain in 1516. The Utopians hold property in common, work six hours a day, practise religious toleration and choose elected officials. The book mixes serious proposal with deliberate ambiguity — More may or may not endorse his fictional society.

More was Lord Chancellor under Henry VIII from 1529 to 1532, resigning over the king's annulment plans. He refused the Oath of Succession (1534) and was executed on 6 July 1535 with the famous 'King's good servant, but God's first.'

He was canonised in 1935. The word 'utopia' entered every European language as a term for an imagined ideal society.
items.why: Renaissance humanism produced political ideas centuries ahead of their reception. 'Utopia' has been read by socialists, anarchists, Catholics and modern progressives — each finding their own programme in More's deliberately ambiguous text.

items.title: The Spanish Armada was defeated partly by the weather
items.claim: How was the Spanish Armada (1588) actually defeated?

options.text: An English naval victory in a single set-piece battle

English fireships at Calais broke the Armada's crescent formation; Gravelines (8 August) inflicted damage; storms in the North Sea and around Scotland and Ireland wrecked perhaps half the surviving ships on the journey home
The Armada turned back before reaching England
Drake destroyed it in a night attack at Cadiz

items.reveal:
The Armada of around 130 ships, led by the Duke of Medina Sidonia, sailed up the Channel in a defensive crescent. Lord Howard of Effingham and Sir Francis Drake harried it but failed to break the formation in open water. On the night of 7-8 August, fireships at Calais panicked the Spanish into cutting their cables.

The Battle of Gravelines (8 August) damaged several galleons. The fleet was driven north into the North Sea; storms around Scotland and the west coast of Ireland wrecked perhaps 35-50 ships. Around 15,000 Spaniards died, mostly from disease, drowning and shipwreck — not English gunfire.

Elizabeth I's commemorative medal read 'Flavit Deus et dissipati sunt' — 'God blew and they were scattered.'
items.why: National myths simplify. The English fleet performed creditably but did not destroy the Armada in battle — wind and disease did most of the killing. The Protestant providential frame was political branding.

items.title: The First Crusade captured Jerusalem with massacre in 1099
items.claim: What happened when the First Crusade took Jerusalem?

options.text: On 15 July 1099 crusaders breached the walls; over the following days a massacre of Muslim and Jewish inhabitants followed — chroniclers (including Raymond of Aguilers) recorded slaughter so extensive that 'one waded in blood up to the ankles'

items.reveal:
The crusade had left Europe in 1096. After taking Antioch (1098), the army of around 14,000 reached Jerusalem in June 1099. The walls were breached on 15 July; the massacre that followed killed thousands. Jewish inhabitants who took refuge in a synagogue were burned alive.

Godfrey of Bouillon was elected 'Defender of the Holy Sepulchre' (refusing the title of king); his brother Baldwin became Baldwin I of Jerusalem in 1100. The Kingdom of Jerusalem lasted until 1291 (fall of Acre).

Saladin recaptured Jerusalem in 1187 with notably less violence — he allowed inhabitants to ransom themselves and many to leave safely, in deliberate contrast to 1099.
items.why: Religious warfare in the high Middle Ages was often atrocious. The 1099 massacre shaped Muslim-Christian relations for centuries — and the comparison with Saladin's 1187 conduct is one that Muslim sources have made repeatedly.
